extracted.intended_audience: students, historians, and readers interested in the history of journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and historical account of the origins and early practice of newspapers and news-letters in England and colonial America, emphasizing production, editorial practices, distribution, censorship, and personalities. Useful for understanding early journalistic standards and institutional context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency and scope of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Harris declares his purpose "to furnish the country once a month with an account of 'such considerable things as have arrived unto our notice'," establishing a clear promise about how often the paper will appear and the kind of material it will cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify publication frequency (e.g., monthly) and commit to covering 'considerable' events of interest to the intended audience; set reader expectations about scope and cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Harris: "nothing shall be entered but what we have reason to believe is true, repairing to the best fountains for our information."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather information from the best available sources; avoid publishing items unless there is reason to believe they are true. This is an explicit verification standard; anti-patterns include relying on unverified gossip or failing to seek primary sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections and error-handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Harris promises: "when there appears any material mistakes in anything that is collected, it shall be corrected in the next."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish timely corrections in subsequent issues when material mistakes are found. Maintain a practice of acknowledging and fixing errors rather than ignoring or hiding them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability for false reports
rubrics_metrics.description: The Publisher offers to "expose the name of such person as a malicious raiser of false report" when he can trace and convict the originator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively trace and identify sources of malicious falsehoods and, where appropriate and safe, publicly name responsible parties. This is both deterrent and corrective; consider legal and ethical risks in naming individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: News selection / 'news-sense'
rubrics_metrics.description: The chapter notes Harris "was not lacking in what is now called news-sense," i.e., the ability to choose and present newsworthy items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate editorial judgment to determine what events are 'considerable' or newsworthy for the readership. Examples: local epidemics, fires, military actions, and notable civic events were selected by early editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing and correspondent responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances where "the correspondent and not the editor" was responsible for omissions such as failing to give names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify responsibility between correspondents and editors for attribution and detail. Encourage correspondents to provide names and specifics; editors should review and require sufficient attribution where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and physical production standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The first issue described as "printed on three pages of a folded sheet... two columns to a page, each page being about eleven by seven inches."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify physical format (page count, columns, size) as part of production standards. Early newspapers followed set physical conventions that affected layout and reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution and organizational channels
rubrics_metrics.description: The text highlights coffee-houses and the postmaster as central distribution and gathering points (e.g., "the postmaster should be the central figure for the trade in gossip" and news being circulated at coffee-clubs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage local social hubs (coffee-houses, post offices) and established networks for gathering and disseminating news. Recognize the institutional role of intermediaries (postmaster, coffee-house keeper) in circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial stance vs. survival strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between Harris's combative editorial stance (willingness to challenge authorities) and Campbell's cautious approach to "publish his paper 'by-authority' and to print nothing that would offend the authorities or religious leaders."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must choose a stance: advocacy/independence may advance public interest but risk suppression, while compliant publishing may ensure longevity but limit critical reporting. Weigh the trade-offs given legal/political context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of censorship and licensing constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities "strictly forbade 'anything in print without license first obtained from those appointed by the government to grant the same'"; licensing acts and censorship repeatedly shaped what could be printed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and plan for legal and licensing constraints in the operating environment. Procedural compliance (obtaining licenses) or strategic resistance (publishing without license) had direct consequences for survival and freedom of the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of news-letters and hybrid formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to the Flying Post, a "half-printed and half-written news-letter" allowing purchasers to "write his own private business or the material news of the day."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider hybrid formats that combine printed material with spaces for local customization or personal notes; adapt formats to reader needs and distribution realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of coffee-houses and clubs in idea circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Coffee-clubs provided receptivity for political ideas and acted as places where politicians and propagandists found audiences, substituting for larger social saloons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social gathering places as both sources of material and channels for audience engagement. Recognize their function as forums for debate and news exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial courage and public-spirited advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The chapter praises traits such as being an "independent and courageous soul," comparing Harris to Zenger and Garrison in willingness to combat authorities for liberty of the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuing independence and willingness to confront power is presented as a journalistic virtue; however, editors must balance advocacy with legal and safety considerations.
